Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette:
Minh Tran is a 76-year-old Vietnamese American man who has worked for the past eleven years as a warehouse worker in a distribution facility outside of Sacramento. He came to the initial intake appointment alone, dressed neatly, and spoke with careful deliberateness, pausing often - not from any difficulty with English, which he has spoken for decades, but from what appeared to be a practiced effort to stay composed. He has never married and lives by himself in a small apartment. He described his reason for seeking help with a kind of exhausted simplicity: he said he was tired of being ambushed by his own mind.

Minh was in his early twenties when his village in the Mekong Delta region became caught in sustained military conflict. He described, over two sessions, a period of several days during which he and other civilians were detained by armed soldiers. He was held in a structure with others, his wrists bound behind him with rope, forced to remain on the ground for hours at a time. The smell of the place - a combination of damp earth, smoke, and what he identified only as "the smell of fear, of bodies" - has stayed with him across five decades with a fidelity that he finds both bewildering and unbearable. At one point during the detention, a confrontation broke out between soldiers near him, and he described the particular quality of that violence - the shouting, the physical proximity, the sense of total helplessness - as the moment he was most certain he would not survive.

He eventually escaped and was resettled in the United States in the late 1970s. For many years, he managed. He worked, kept to himself, and described a kind of deliberate forward momentum that served him well enough. But the symptoms he now presents with have intensified over the past two years, and he connects this, without being entirely sure why, to the slower pace and greater solitude that have come with aging.

The triggers Minh encounters are specific and, in the context of his history, entirely coherent. At the warehouse, he works in receiving, where deliveries are unloaded and sorted. The job occasionally requires him to maneuver in tight spaces between shelving units, and twice in the past year a coworker has grabbed his arm or shoulder from behind without warning - once to redirect him away from a moving forklift. Both times, the physical sensation of being held or constrained sent him immediately back into the detention. Something in his surroundings can, without any transition or preparation, collapse the distance between Sacramento and the Mekong Delta entirely. A smell - diesel exhaust mixed with damp concrete, or occasionally the particular odor of certain packing materials - does the same. When a coworker raised his voice during a dispute over a shipment manifest last spring, Minh felt the confrontation not as a workplace annoyance but as something physically threatening, and the memory of the soldiers arguing over him returned with full force.

What makes these intrusions so destabilizing is not only their vividness - and they are vivid, detailed in ways that feel less like remembering than reliving - but the emotional weight they carry. When the memory returns, Minh described feeling so overwhelmed that he has to stop what he is doing entirely, sometimes stepping outside the warehouse and sitting on a loading dock until the feeling passes. He has begun arriving earlier than his shift requires so he can orient himself to the space before others arrive, and he has quietly rearranged his work patterns to avoid the tight aisles where he feels most confined.

The memory itself, once activated, seems to heighten his sensitivity to the very cues that provoked it. After an intrusion, Minh finds himself scanning for smells, watching for raised voices, and bracing against any physical proximity - as though the memory, having surfaced, leaves him primed for the next trigger. He has become somewhat withdrawn from his coworkers, and his supervisor has noted the change without understanding it.

What brought him finally to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when, after being startled by a coworker's touch, he sat on the loading dock and realized he could not remember, for several minutes, what year it was. What he most hopes for, he said quietly, is simply to feel like the past is the past.
